adventure.title: Guardians of the Ancient City
adventure.description: St. Augustine is watched over by stone and bronze sentinels — explorers, priests, founders, and lions that stand at the city's oldest corners. A mysterious collector has erased the identities of the city's historic figures and guardians. Restore each identity by finding statues, monuments, busts, and sculptural details across the bayfront, plaza, and beyond.
adventure.short_description: Find the statues and monuments that guard the Ancient City.

stops.title: Bridge of Lions — The Marble Guardians
stops.description: The twin marble lions at the western approach of the Bridge of Lions are among the most photographed objects in St. Augustine. The bridge connects the historic downtown to Anastasia Island across the Matanzas River. The lions were installed when the bridge opened in 1927 and restored during the bridge's reconstruction in the 2000s. The name of the bridge is itself a tribute — and a pun on the name of the explorer Juan Ponce de León, whose last name means lion.
stops.historical_content:
The Bridge of Lions opened to traffic on February 26, 1927. Dr. Andrew Anderson, who donated many of St. Augustine's landmarks, gifted the bridge its name and its marble lions. On June 10, 1924, Dr. Anderson requested the city council to name the new bridge either 'Ponce de Leon' or 'Bridge of Lions.' The lion connection is deliberate: Leon = lion in Spanish, linking the bridge to Juan Ponce de León, Florida's first European explorer.

Juan Ponce de León, whose statue stands near the plaza, discovered Florida on March 27, 1513. He gave the territory its name: Pascua de Flores (Land of Flowers) in honor of his Easter arrival. His statue in St. Augustine is a duplicate of the Ponce de León statue in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and was donated by Dr. Andrew Anderson.

The marble lions on the bridge are Medici lions — a classical style originating in Florence, Italy. Each lion rests its paw on a sphere. The original sculptor of the Medici lion design was Flaminio Vacca in the 16th century; the St. Augustine versions are 20th-century reproductions in that tradition.
stops.hint_text: Walk to the western end of the Bridge of Lions — the drawbridge over the Matanzas River at the foot of Cathedral Place.
stops.safety_warning: Stay on the pedestrian walkway. Do not lean over the railing.

challenges.prompt: Each marble lion at the Bridge of Lions rests one paw on an object. What is it?
challenges.hint_text: Look directly beneath the raised paw of either lion — it's a classic sculptural motif called a Medici lion.

config.explanation: Each lion rests its paw on a sphere — a classic motif of the Medici lion, a sculptural tradition originating in 16th-century Florence. The name of the bridge is a pun on Juan Ponce de León: León means lion in Spanish.

challenges.prompt: The bridge is named 'Bridge of Lions.' Which Spanish explorer's last name also means 'lion' in Spanish — connecting the bridge's name to Florida's history?
challenges.hint_text: He 'discovered' Florida on March 27, 1513 — his last name literally means lion.

config.explanation: Juan Ponce de León — León means lion in Spanish. Dr. Andrew Anderson, who donated the lions and the bridge's name, made the connection deliberate. His statue stands near the Plaza de la Constitución.

stops.title: Plaza de la Constitución — Ponce de León and the Founder
stops.description: Two important statues are near this plaza. The statue of Juan Ponce de León stands at the eastern end of the plaza near the Bridge of Lions — he faces the bay he first encountered in 1513. Nearby on the bayfront, the bronze statue of Pedro Menéndez de Avilés commemorates the man who actually founded St. Augustine on September 8, 1565. Find both, read the inscriptions, and figure out what each figure is holding.
stops.historical_content:
Juan Ponce de León sighted Florida on March 27, 1513 — calling it Pascua de Flores (Land of Flowers) for its Easter timing. He gave Florida its name. His St. Augustine statue is a duplicate of the one in San Juan, Puerto Rico, donated by Dr. Andrew Anderson.

Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine on September 8, 1565 — not to build a city for its own sake, but for three strategic reasons: to counter the French Protestant colony at Fort Caroline (today's Jacksonville), to protect Spanish treasure ships using the Gulf Stream, and to convert the Timucuan people to Catholicism. He sighted Florida from his ship Pearl on August 28, the Feast Day of Saint Augustine — which is how the city received its name.

Menéndez was one of the most ruthless and effective commanders in Spanish imperial history. On September 20, 1565 he captured Fort Caroline and renamed it Fort San Mateo. At Matanzas Inlet, nearly 250 French Protestants were slaughtered — giving the inlet its Spanish name: Matanzas (slaughters).

The plaza itself has been a public space since the Spanish colonial era. The Constitution Monument in the center was erected in 1813 to honor the Spanish Constitution of 1812. Geronimo Alvarez, the mayor and owner of the Oldest House, refused to allow it to be demolished when Florida was transferred to the United States — making it possibly the only surviving monument honoring that constitution.
stops.hint_text: Walk to the Plaza de la Constitución — the open plaza between King Street and Cathedral Place, with the Constitution Monument in its center. The Ponce de León statue is at the east end near the bay.

challenges.title: Why Did Menéndez Found St. Augustine?
challenges.prompt: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés had three stated goals when he founded St. Augustine in 1565. Which of the following was NOT one of them?
challenges.hint_text: His three goals were military, economic, and religious — think about what a Spanish conquistador in 1565 would have been trying to accomplish.

options: To drive out the French Protestant colony at Fort Caroline
To protect Spanish treasure ships using the Gulf Stream
To establish a permanent tobacco trading post
To convert the Timucuan people to the Catholic faith
config.explanation: Menéndez had three goals: defeat the French at Fort Caroline, protect Spanish treasure ships traveling the Gulf Stream back to Spain, and convert the Native Americans to Catholicism. Tobacco trade was not among his stated missions.

challenges.title: The City's Name
challenges.prompt: St. Augustine is named for the Christian bishop and theologian Saint Augustine of Hippo. But why was the city given that particular name on that particular day?
challenges.hint_text: Menéndez sighted land from his ship Pearl on a specific feast day in the Catholic calendar.

options: Pedro Menéndez was born on Saint Augustine's feast day
Menéndez sighted Florida on August 28, the Feast Day of Saint Augustine
The King of Spain ordered all new colonies named for saints
The first church built was dedicated to Saint Augustine
config.explanation: Menéndez sighted land from his ship Pearl on August 28, 1565 — the Feast Day of Saint Augustine of Hippo. When he formally founded the settlement on September 8, 1565, the saint's name was already attached to the site. Saint Augustine is also the patron saint of Aviles, Spain, Menéndez's hometown.

challenges.title: Bonus: Speak with the Founder
challenges.prompt: Speak with Pedro Menéndez de Avilés about the founding of St. Augustine. Ask him why he came, what he found, and what he wanted to build.
challenges.hint_text: Ask about the French at Fort Caroline, or about his first days after landing on September 8, 1565.

stops.title: Cathedral Basilica — Father Camps
stops.description: The Cathedral Basilica of St. Augustine is the seat of the oldest Catholic parish in the United States, with records dating to a baptism on June 10, 1594. At the entrance stands an 8-foot bronze statue of Father Pedro Camps — the Minorcan priest who held his community together through decades of hardship. The statue was sculpted by Joseph Viladomat of Barcelona and dedicated in 1975. Find it, read the inscription, and learn who the Minorcans were and why their priest stands at this cathedral.
stops.historical_content:
Father Pedro Camps arrived in Florida in 1768 as the priest of a group of Minorcan, Greek, Italian, and Corsican indentured workers recruited by Dr. Andrew Turnbull for a plantation at New Smyrna Beach. The plantation failed, the workers were mistreated, and by 1777 most had walked to St. Augustine to seek their freedom. The courts freed them from their contracts.

Father Camps was the glue that held the Minorcan community together. He kept the births, deaths, and marriages of the community in a book still known as the Golden Book of the Minorcans. He kept the Catholic faith alive in St. Augustine through the British Period (1763-1783), when there was no official Spanish Catholic presence. November 9, 1777 was the date the last Minorcans left New Smyrna and joined their community in St. Augustine.

The Cathedral itself was started in 1793 in Spanish mission style. The original architect was Mariano de la Rocque. The contractor was Don Miguel Ysnardy. It was dedicated on December 8, 1797 — the Feast of the Immaculate Conception. Three people are buried inside: Father Camps, Don Miguel Ysnardy, and Father Font. The Cathedral building incorporates stones from three earlier churches that were demolished to build it: Nombre de Dios, Nuestra Senora de Guadalupe de Tolomato, and Nuestra Senora de la Soledad.

By 1819, an observer noted that the city's population of 5,000 was 'principally Minorcans and natives of the province' — the community Father Camps built.
stops.hint_text: Walk to the Cathedral Basilica on Cathedral Place — the large church with the bell tower facing the plaza. The statue of Father Camps stands near the entrance.
stops.safety_warning: Please be respectful. Mass may be in progress. Photography is generally permitted in exterior areas.

challenges.title: The Golden Book
challenges.prompt: Father Camps kept careful records of the Minorcan community through decades of hardship. What is the name of the book he maintained — which still survives today?
challenges.hint_text: It's a precious record of births, deaths, and marriages in the Minorcan community — and its name reflects how it's been treasured.

options: The Silver Register of St. Augustine
The Golden Book of the Minorcans
The Camps Parish Journal
The New Smyrna Ledger
config.explanation: Father Camps kept the births, deaths, and marriages of the Minorcan community in what is now called the Golden Book of the Minorcans — a document that survives to this day as one of the earliest community records in Florida.

challenges.title: Inside the Cathedral
challenges.prompt: Three people are buried inside the Cathedral Basilica itself. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
challenges.hint_text: The three burials are a priest, a building contractor, and another priest who died very young after arriving. Check the historical plaques inside if you're unsure.

options: Father Pedro Camps
Don Miguel Ysnardy (the building contractor)
Father Font
Pedro Menéndez de Avilés
config.explanation: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés is not buried in the Cathedral — he is buried in Spain. The three people buried inside the Cathedral Basilica are Father Pedro Camps, Don Miguel Ysnardy (the building's contractor), and Father Font, who died on January 13, 1793, within a year of his arrival.

challenges.prompt: Ask the guide about the Minorcans — who they were, how they got to St. Augustine, and why Father Camps' statue stands at this cathedral.

stops.title: Mission Nombre de Dios — Father López and the Great Cross
stops.description: The Mission Nombre de Dios on San Marco Avenue marks the spot where Pedro Menéndez de Avilés first landed on September 8, 1565 — the founding moment of St. Augustine. A statue of Father Francisco López de Mendoza Grajales stands here. He was the chaplain who celebrated the first Mass in what would become the United States and kept a diary of the landing. Behind him rises the Great Cross — a 208-foot stainless steel cross erected in 1966 for the 400th anniversary of the city's founding.
stops.historical_content:
Father Francisco López de Mendoza Grajales was the chaplain aboard Pedro Menéndez's fleet. He celebrated the first Mass in St. Augustine on September 8, 1565, and kept a diary of the landing — one of the most important primary sources for the founding of the city.

The Mission Nombre de Dios (Mission of the Name of God) was established here by the Franciscans in 1587. By 1678 it was constructed of stone by Governor Hita Salazar. The mission became associated with the Virgin Mary and was called Nuestra Senora de la Leche y Buen Parto (Our Lady of Milk and Good Birth).

Over the course of the Spanish colonial period, more than 300 Franciscan friars baptized approximately 170,000 Native Americans from missions across the Southeast, using St. Augustine as their base.

The 208-foot stainless steel Great Cross was designed by artist Ivan Mestrovic and erected on October 30, 1966 for the 400th anniversary of the founding. The cross is illuminated at night and visible from much of the surrounding area.
stops.hint_text: Walk north on San Marco Avenue to the Mission Nombre de Dios — the shrine with the towering stainless steel cross. The statue of Father López is near the chapel.
stops.safety_warning: This is an active Catholic shrine. Please be respectful.

stops.title: City Gate — The Stone Sentinels
stops.description: The two white coquina pillars at the north end of St. George Street are the City Gate — the only surviving gateway into the walled Spanish colonial city. Built in 1808 during the Second Spanish Period, these pillars replaced a wooden gate called La Leche Gate that had stood since 1739. Each pillar is 14 feet high, capped with a pomegranate — the symbol of fertility and of the city of Granada, Spain. The gate is also known as the Land Gate, distinguishing it from the sea approach via the harbor.
stops.historical_content:
The current City Gate was built in 1808 under the engineering supervision of Captain Manuel de Hita, who recommended a masonry replacement for the wooden guard houses. The two four-foot-square coquina pillars frame an opening 12 feet wide. Each pillar is 14 feet high. The twin towers of white masonry were trimmed with red plaster and each roof was capped with a pomegranate — the symbol of fertility and of Granada, Spain.

The gate was completed in 1818 with the addition of stone guardhouses and pomegranate decorations by Francisco de Cortazar.

The Cubo Line — the defensive earthwork that connected to the gate — was first built in 1704-05 and rebuilt in 1737. It ran from the Castillo to the San Sebastian River, protecting the northern approach to the city. The area just inside the gate was where the British burned St. Augustine's wooden buildings during the Drake Raid of 1586.

St. George Street itself is named after King George III — the only British landmark in St. Augustine that almost every tourist experiences today. The street was the main commercial and residential corridor throughout the colonial period.
stops.hint_text: Walk to the northern end of St. George Street — the pedestrian zone. The City Gate is the pair of white coquina pillars framing the entrance.

challenges.prompt: The City Gate marks the northern entrance to the walled colonial city. Which defensive line connected to this gate, protecting the land approach to St. Augustine?

options: The Matanzas Wall
The Rosario Line
The Cubo Line
The Drake Redoubt
config.explanation: The Cubo Line — a defensive earthwork first built in 1704-05 and rebuilt in 1737 — ran from the Castillo de San Marcos to the San Sebastian River, protecting the northern land approach. The City Gate was the opening in this defensive perimeter.
